Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X In this article Gemini 4 Carbon is available Higher-precision knowledge work Improved agentic coding State-of-the-art cybersecurity Frontier-level scientific reasoning Progress in model safety and security Getting started Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports. Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model. Using Google Antigravity’s new /swarm feature, a team of Gemini 4 Carbon agents turned historical photos and engineering plates into an interactive Three.js 3D exhibition of the Eiffel Tower's 1887–1889 construction from a single prompt. With seven public City Council planning PDFs (206 extracted engineering drawing views) and a single prompt, a multi-agent Carbon team using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature built an interactive 906K-triangle Three.js reconstruction of Google’s Platform 37 office across 10 overnight loops. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Carbon built an interactive multiscale textile visualizer based on an academic paper, modeling a virtual-fiber finite element framework with interactive 3D yarn meshes, 110-fiber polar tracking, and dynamic stress-strain curves with minimal prompting. In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding. Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding. Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music. Try the live app . Paired with improved front end taste and motion design skills in Google Antigravity, Carbon reimagined the Google Merchandise Store in two prompts, proposing five art direction concepts and generating all-new product imagery with Nano Banana 2.1. Try the live app and Gemini front end design skill . Starting from a video reference generated with Gemini Omni in Google Antigravity, built a cinematic multi-shot underwater Atlantis scene. The pipeline modeled procedural ruins, volumetric caustic lighting, and water simulation in Blender before converting the full environment to Three.js for real-time browser rendering. Using a multi-agent loop in Google Antigravity, Carbon reconstructed a playable c. 1780 Stein-Schule fortepiano with 61-key escapement physics from CAD drawings and X-ray radiographs and placed it in a 3D model of the Royal Conservatory of Music's Koerner Hall in Toronto with seat-specific spatial acoustics. Try the live app . Frontier cybersecurity capabilities Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches. Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice. In Project Fortify , Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem. Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit . By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes. As part of Wiz’s Scan for Good program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies. Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning Gemini 4 Carbon shows strongly improved performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences, synthesizing experimental data, testing hypotheses, and reasoning through multi-step domain problems. For drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio, Carbon is now the leading model in performance for translational science, finding novel mechanisms of toxicity they hadn’t found previously. Axiom is now moving their production scientific analyses and agents to both Carbon and Argon to unlock the creation of safer drugs. Researchers across Google have been using Carbon in Google Antigravity to accelerate their work: Code verification: Researchers built a new agentic framework for formal verification called AlphaProof Code and put it to work on a major security challenge: mathematically proving the actual code underlying the cryptographic protocol of Signal . Using Carbon alongside other models, our researchers translated security goals to mathematical theorems. AlphaProof Code agents then used Carbon to generate millions of lines of code in Lean, a computer language for writing mathematical proofs, helping them prove key security properties in weeks — a task that historically takes expert teams years. The result indicates Carbon’s potential to unlock scalable formal verification, long considered a gold-standard approach to building secure software. Enzyme assay development : Provided with only lab notebooks and raw data, Carbon went beyond standard analysis to surface hard-to-interpret data anomalies, which it used to diagnose subtle wet lab experimental artifacts such as incomplete automated mixing in deep wells, leading to substantially improved reproducibility. Moreover Carbon improved methods to deconvolute chromatography peaks and caught trace sample carryover in research instruments, significantly accelerating the development of new assays and tightening the feedback loop between computation and the bench. Protein structure prediction: Structure prediction models like AlphaFold 3 use Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) of evolutionary relatives to help infer how amino acid chains fold. As a result they often struggle on understudied, viral, microbial, and eukaryotic proteins that have very few matches in standard databases. Working in a multi-agent setup, our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon to autonomously discover remote homologs across petabase-scale unannotated sequence archives, environmental and viral sequence catalogs, and 3D structure databases. For example, across 7 low-homolog protein families from the CASP17 blind test set, Carbon increased the number of homologs retrieved by 40-fold on average, greatly increasing the information available to structure prediction models without need for retraining. While broader benchmarking is still underway, addressing this upstream search bottleneck potentially offers a promising path toward modeling hard-to-characterize regions of the proteome. Four weeks ago, we opened applications to give 10,000 scientists access to Argon in Google Antigravity free of charge for six months to accelerate the pace of their research, and we’ve onboarded thousands of scientists already. Today, we’re expanding access to Carbon for current and future participants, and going forward, the program will continue providing access to our latest frontier models as they become available. Applications remain open and onboarding continues on a weekly rolling basis, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. Progress in model safety and security With each new model release, we continue to strengthen our safety and security mitigations, agentic misuse prevention, model alignment, and harm reduction proportionately with model capability. Because Gemini 4 Carbon introduces stronger cyber capabilities we build on Argon’s strong safety and security stack to fortify robustness to misuse and prompt injection. Mitigating frontier safety misuse risks: We’ve strengthened our misuse safeguards to help ensure stronger defensive reasoning does not translate into offensive risk. In simulated cyberattack testing environments seeded with ExploitBench and CyScenarioBench, Carbon blocked 99% of attack trajectories from our adaptive red-teaming agent that can iteratively revisit its attack plans after each block. The Carbon safeguards lowered the per-attempt breach rate to just 0.8% (down from 3.1% on Argon). Our safeguards also lowered the automated cyberattack query success rate to 2.17% in Gray Swan’s testing, compared to 9.86% on Argon. And external testing by Trajectory Labs found zero new universal jailbreaks across 132 hours and over 13,000 requests. Promoting safe and aligned model interactions: When we announced Carbon, we showed significant improvements in alignment as measured by our monitor flag rates across the model’s lifecycle, as well as reductions in data fabrication. New results show that on our 375-task agentic honesty benchmark, it passed 92% of tasks (compared to 70% for Argon) — declining to fill in missing experimental data 98% of the time and flagging methodological flaws 68% of the time. Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: Two weeks ago, we shared that Carbon achieved a 0% prompt injection attack success rate on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark — marking the first time that milestone has been reached. At the same time, we know that prompt injection robustness remains an area for continued improvement. Our advanced automated red teaming continues to push the limits here and has shown that models could be further improved against sophisticated attacks in some distributions. It provides the data for us to continuously advance our models’ security to the next frontier. For more details, read the full Gemini 4 Carbon Safety and Security report . Getting started with Gemini 4 Carbon Starting today, Carbon joins Argon in our family of frontier models across our products: For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in AI Studio and Android Studio , and if you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity and AI Studio. For enterprises: Try it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, or CodeMender. For everyday users: Try Carbon starting today in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search if you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber. For scientists & researchers: Apply for a chance to get access to both Argon and Carbon via Google Antigravity’s highest usage tier free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. For cybersecurity defenders: Apply to join the Fairwind Program to get access to Carbon for cyber on a rolling basis. See the model card to learn more about Gemini 4 Carbon and to start building with it, explore our updated Gemini 4 developer guide and documentation for best practices on migrating workflows to the model. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report for Argon . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. Gemini is one universal agent for the way you work. When using Gemini at work, it operates across your email, docs, code, data, and business apps across web, desktop, and mobile, so you can hand off the work instead of supervising it. There is no platform to stand up and no agent to assemble: you turn it on and it starts working with what you already have from the same prompt box, with the same shared context. Do I have to move our data into Google? No. Gemini indexes selected sources while keeping data where it lives, and access strictly follows each user's existing permissions. Over 100 supported integrations like Google Workspace (Docs, Gmail, and Drive), Microsoft 365 (Outlook, Teams, and OneDrive), Slack, Confluence, Notion, Jira, Linear, Monday, Asana, Smartsheet, GitHub, GitLab, Salesforce, HubSpot, ServiceNow, Docusign, and BigQuery. Who owns our data, and does Google use my data to train models? When using Gemini for your business, Gemini is built on Google Cloud’s secure-by-design infrastructure, giving you the peace of mind to deploy AI across your organization confidently: You own your data, not Google Your data, including prompts, outputs, and model tuning, is never used to train Google models or models for any other customer Google never sells customer data to third parties Google doesn’t use customer data for advertising What does Gemini remember about me? Session memory for active tasks, semantic memory for structured business knowledge, procedural memory for workflows, and episodic memory of past actions across devices and channels. Lengthy jobs also run on their own secure machine in Google Cloud, so even if you log off for the day, Gemini has the work done when you get back. Which models can I use? Google Gemini models today, with additional models coming soon. Gemini uses automated routing to select the optimal model for speed, cost, and accuracy, all under one set of permissions and one bill. How can I try Gemini for my business? You can get started by contacting Google Cloud sales, or try Gemini Enterprise Plus edition at no cost for 30 days without sales assistance. Anthropic Open in Claude The User-Pays Model means your users cover their own cloud and AI usage, instead of you, the developer. Each user pays for the resources they consume in your app through their own Puter account. Whether you have 1 or 1 million users, your infrastructure cost stays at $0. How it works Users sign in to your app with their Puter account, and that account covers the AI, storage, and other resources they use. Their usage never touches your bill. Every user starts with a free monthly allowance, enough to test out the platform and use apps built with Puter.js. They can track their usage in the usage dashboard . If a user runs out of their allowance, Puter prompts them to upgrade for more, or they can do it themselves in their billing settings . When you, as a developer, use your own app, you are also subject to the User-Pays Model: you cover your own usage like any other user. User-Pays Model vs. Traditional Model Traditional Puter.js Servers & databases You set up and pay None needed API keys You manage and secure them No API keys at all Billing You pay for all users' usage Each user pays their own Scaling Costs grow with users Zero cost at any scale Abuse protection Rate limits, CAPTCHAs, quotas Not needed; abusers pay for themselves Advantages Zero infrastructure costs : no server, AI, or API bills, at any scale. Perfect for vibe coding : build and ship apps with AI without fear of a surprise bill. If your app goes viral overnight, each user still covers their own usage. No API keys : no keys to buy, secure, or ask your users to bring. Built-in auth & security : users sign in with Puter; your app runs within the permissions they grant. No anti-abuse code : bad actors pay for their own usage, so there's no incentive to abuse your app. Simpler codebase : cloud and AI are handled by Puter.js, so many apps can be frontend-only. Better UX : single sign-on and unified billing through the user's existing Puter account. OpenRouter enforces three kinds of limits: Limit type What it governs Error on exceeding Where to check Credit limits How much you can spend (account balance, per-key credit caps, and the in-flight spending budget) GET /api/v1/key → limit_remaining ; error.metadata.limit_source on the error response Budget limits Spend caps an org admin configured: guardrail budgets, workspace budgets, and the key’s own limit once it is spent GET /api/v1/key → budgets and effective_budget ; error.metadata on the error response Rate limits How many requests you can make (free-model request caps, key-management caps, per-IP burst limits, and DDoS protection) X-RateLimit-* headers on free-model and key-management errors ​ Checking your limits To check the rate limit or credits left on an API key, make a GET request to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/key . If you submit a valid API key, you should get a response of the form: TypeScript // One budget that applies to requests made with the key (see Budget limits below) type Budget = { scope : 'workspace_default_member' | 'workspace_default_key' | 'member' | 'api_key' | 'workspace' | 'key_limit' ; guardrail_id : string | null ; // Set for guardrail scopes budget_id : string | null ; // Set for the workspace scope limit_usd : number ; spend_usd : number ; // Spend counted against the limit in the current window remaining_usd : number ; // limit_usd - spend_usd; zero or negative blocks requests reset_interval : 'daily' | 'weekly' | 'monthly' | null ; // null never resets resets_at : string | null ; // ISO 8601 UTC instant the window rolls over, or null include_byok : boolean ; // Whether external BYOK spend counts toward this budget }; type Key = { data : { label : string ; limit : number | null ; // Credit limit for the key, or null if unlimited limit_reset : string | null ; // Type of limit reset for the key, or null if never resets limit_remaining : number | null ; // Remaining credits for the key, or null if unlimited include_byok_in_limit : boolean ; // Whether to include external BYOK usage in the credit limit budgets : Budget []; // Every budget enforced for this key, in the order enforcement checks them effective_budget : Budget | null ; // The budget that blocks requests first, or null if none usage : number ; // Number of credits used (all time) usage_daily : number ; // Number of credits used (current UTC day) usage_weekly : number ; // ... (current UTC week, starting Monday) usage_monthly : number ; // ... (current UTC month) byok_usage : number ; // Same for external BYOK usage byok_usage_daily : number ; byok_usage_weekly : number ; byok_usage_monthly : number ; is_free_tier : boolean ; // Whether the user has paid for credits before free_model_daily_requests : { used : number ; // Free-model requests recorded so far in the current UTC day limit : number ; // Free-model requests allowed per UTC day (see the free usage limits below) remaining : number ; // Free-model requests left in the current UTC day }; // rate_limit: { ... } // A deprecated object in the response, safe to ignore }; }; See all 44 lines ​ Credit limits Credit limits govern how much you can spend. They come from three places: Account balance , your available credits across the account. If your account has a negative credit balance, you may see errors, including for free models. Adding credits to put your balance above zero allows you to use those models again. Per-key credit limits , an optional spending cap configured on an individual API key. The limit , limit_reset , and limit_remaining fields in the GET /api/v1/key response above describe this cap and how much of it remains. In-flight spending budget , a cap on the estimated token cost of the paid requests you have running or recently completed, relative to your balance. See In-flight spending budget below. ​ In-flight spending budget OpenRouter charges a request when it finishes, so many requests running at the same time could commit more than your balance covers before any of them settles. To prevent that, OpenRouter estimates each paid request’s token cost up front, at the endpoint’s prices: the input tokens, plus the completion tokens allowed by max_tokens up to a fixed per-request cap (the cap is used when max_tokens is not set). Only token prices are estimated; per-request fees, plugin charges, and image pricing are not part of the estimate, so a request whose cost has no token component is not held. The estimate is held against your account while the request runs. When the request completes or fails, the hold is replaced by the request’s actual cost for a short settlement window, and then released. The total that can be held at once is your in-flight spending budget: a fraction of your current credit balance, up to a fixed ceiling. A request whose estimated cost does not fit alongside your running and recently completed requests is rejected with before it reaches a provider, even though your balance is positive. The error’s metadata says which case you hit: "reason": "in_flight_budget_exhausted" with "limit_source": "openrouter_in_flight_budget" : your running and recently completed requests already fill the budget. This is transient and can occur with no request still running, while recent costs are settling. The response includes a Retry-After header; wait for it and retry. "reason": "weight_exceeds_budget" with "limit_source": "openrouter_credits" : this single request’s estimated cost is larger than your whole budget, so retrying will not help. Lower max_tokens or the prompt size, or add credits. Every whose metadata carries limit_source also carries remedy_hint , a one-line human-readable next step for that source. It is meant for people reading logs; branch on limit_source , not on the hint text. { "error" : { "code" : 402 , "message" : "This request would exceed your available credits given your current in-flight requests. Retry after in-flight requests settle, or add credits." , "metadata" : { "reason" : "in_flight_budget_exhausted" , "limit_source" : "openrouter_in_flight_budget" , "remedy_hint" : "Retry after your in-flight requests settle (see the Retry-After header). Adding credits at https://openrouter.ai/settings/credits raises your in-flight budget, up to a capped ceiling." } } } The budget applies to prepaid accounts spending their own credits, and only to a subset of them: accounts whose balance is below a threshold, and, while the mechanism is being rolled out, newer accounts without an established spending history. A larger balance raises the budget up to the ceiling, and a balance at or above the threshold is not subject to it at all. It does not apply to requests to free models, to requests served entirely with your own provider keys (see BYOK ) that use no paid plugins, or to enterprise, paid-subscription, or invoice-billed accounts. ​ Handling 402 errors To resolve errors: Check error.metadata.limit_source in the response body. openrouter_in_flight_budget means your running and recently completed requests filled your in-flight spending budget , not your balance: wait for the Retry-After header and retry. openrouter_key_limit means the API key’s credit limit is exhausted. openrouter_credits means your balance cannot cover the request, or the single request is too expensive for your in-flight budget. Add credits to bring your account balance above zero, or to raise your in-flight spending budget. Check per-key limits. If limit_remaining on the key is exhausted, raise the key’s credit limit or wait for it to reset (see limit_reset ). Reduce the request size (fewer input tokens or a lower max_tokens ) so its estimated cost fits your balance and in-flight budget. Monitor proactively. Call GET /api/v1/key as shown above to track limit_remaining and usage before requests start failing. ​ Budget limits Budget limits are spend caps an org admin configures. They come from three places, and OpenRouter checks them in this order on every paid request, so the first one that is spent is the one that blocks: Guardrail budgets : a limit_usd with a reset_interval on the workspace default guardrail (checked against the member’s combined spend, then against the key’s own spend), on the guardrail assigned to the member, and on the guardrail assigned to the API key. See Guardrails . Workspace budgets : caps on the whole workspace’s spend per interval. See Workspace budgets . The key’s own limit : the limit field above, once its window is spent. Spend windows are UTC: a daily budget resets at 00:00 UTC, a weekly one on Monday 00:00 UTC, a monthly one on the first of the month 00:00 UTC. A lifetime workspace budget never resets. ​ Checking your budgets GET /api/v1/key lists every budget that applies to the key in budgets , with the spend enforcement counts against it, how much is left, and when the window rolls over. effective_budget is the budget that blocks requests first: when one is already spent it is the entry enforcement rejects on (the first in the order above, or the broadest spent workspace budget), otherwise it is the entry with the least remaining_usd . limit and limit_remaining keep describing only the key’s own limit. GET /api/v1/key (excerpt) { "data" : { "limit" : null , "limit_remaining" : null , "budgets" : [ { "scope" : "workspace_default_member" , "guardrail_id" : "0df9e665-d932-5740-b2c7-b52af166bc11" , "budget_id" : null , "limit_usd" : 100 , "spend_usd" : 40 , "remaining_usd" : 60 , "reset_interval" : "weekly" , "resets_at" : "2026-10-12T00:00:00.000Z" , "include_byok" : false }, { "scope" : "member" , "guardrail_id" : "6b1d2c3e-4f50-4a61-9b72-83c4d5e6f708" , "budget_id" : null , "limit_usd" : 50 , "spend_usd" : 40 , "remaining_usd" : 10 , "reset_interval" : "weekly" , "resets_at" : "2026-10-12T00:00:00.000Z" , "include_byok" : false } ], "effective_budget" : { "scope" : "member" , "guardrail_id" : "6b1d2c3e-4f50-4a61-9b72-83c4d5e6f708" , "budget_id" : null , "limit_usd" : 50 , "spend_usd" : 40 , "remaining_usd" : 10 , "reset_interval" : "weekly" , "resets_at" : "2026-10-12T00:00:00.000Z" , "include_byok" : false } } } ​ Handling 403 budget errors A request that a budget blocks fails with before it reaches a provider. The message names the budget and ends with the figures, and error.metadata carries them as fields: { "error" : { "code" : 403 , "message" : "Org member budget limit exceeded (weekly limit). Contact your org admin. $52.00 of $50.00 used; resets 2026-10-12T00:00:00.000Z." , "metadata" : { "limit_source" : "openrouter_guardrail_budget" , "remedy_hint" : "Wait for the budget window to reset (see metadata.resets_at), or ask your org admin to raise the guardrail budget." , "scope" : "member" , "limit_usd" : 50 , "spend_usd" : 52 , "resets_at" : "2026-10-12T00:00:00.000Z" } } } limit_source is openrouter_guardrail_budget for a guardrail budget, openrouter_workspace_budget for a workspace budget, and openrouter_key_limit for the key’s own limit. scope matches the scope values in GET /api/v1/key , so you can find the same entry in budgets . resets_at is the ISO 8601 UTC instant the window rolls over, or null for a lifetime workspace budget. Retrying before it will fail the same way; there is no Retry-After header because the wait is usually hours or days. Call GET /api/v1/key before a long task and watch effective_budget.remaining_usd to avoid hitting the cap partway through. ​ Rate limits Rate limits govern how many requests you can make. There are a few rate limits that apply to certain types of requests, regardless of account status: Free usage limits : If you’re using a free model variant (with an ID ending in : ), the following limits apply: Credits purchased (all time) Requests per minute Requests per day Less than At least The free_model_daily_requests field in the GET /api/v1/key response above reports the daily counter and ceiling that gate your free-model requests when these limits apply to your account. Accounts and endpoints exempt from free-model limits, and BYOK requests, are not gated by it, so remaining reflects the tier policy rather than an enforced ceiling for them. The per-minute limit is not reported there. The limit tier is selected by all-time credits purchased, independently of is_free_tier . To absorb rounding and top-up fees, the higher daily ceiling is granted starting one credit below the table’s threshold (currently credits); an account that has purchased fewer credits than that reports is_free_tier: false together with the lower daily ceiling. Key-management limits : Creating, updating, and deleting API keys with a management key count toward a daily limit for your account or organization. The limit is 10,000 requests per day by default, and it resets at 00:00 UTC. POST /api/v1/keys , PATCH /api/v1/keys/{hash} (including disabling a key), and DELETE /api/v1/keys/{hash} all count toward the same limit. A request counts even if it then fails, for example with a 404 for an unknown key. Reading keys, usage, or credits doesn’t count toward it. When you reach the limit, requests fail with until the reset. The X-RateLimit-Reset header gives the reset time in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. If you create a short-lived key for each job, set expires_at when you create it instead of deleting it afterward. This halves the requests that count toward the limit. If your workload needs a higher limit, contact support. Per-IP burst limits : These endpoints also limit how many requests each client IP address can make per minute: Key writes: POST /api/v1/keys , PATCH /api/v1/keys/{hash} , and DELETE /api/v1/keys/{hash} Key reads: GET /api/v1/keys and GET /api/v1/keys/{hash} Current key and credits: GET /api/v1/key and GET /api/v1/credits Each endpoint counts separately, except that PATCH and DELETE on /api/v1/keys/{hash} share a count. The limits for key writes are lower than the limits for the other endpoints. These responses don’t include X-RateLimit-* headers, so wait a few seconds and retry with exponential backoff. DDoS protection : Cloudflare’s DDoS protection will block requests that dramatically exceed reasonable usage. ​ Handling 429 errors Requests rejected with fail with a standard error response : { "error" : { "code" : 429 , "message" : "Rate limit exceeded" , "metadata" : { "error_type" : "rate_limit_exceeded" } } } A error can come from two places: OpenRouter , when you hit one of the platform limits above (free-model requests per minute or per day, key-management requests per day, per-IP burst limits, or DDoS protection). The upstream provider , when the provider serving your request is rate limiting or at capacity. In this case error.metadata.provider_code carries the provider’s original error code when available, and fallback routing retries other providers for the same model automatically before the error reaches you. You can also specify fallback models to try a different model when all providers for the first are exhausted. Successful inference responses do not include X-RateLimit-* headers. When OpenRouter itself returns a error for a free-model or key-management limit, the error response carries X-RateLimit-Limit , X-RateLimit-Remaining , and X-RateLimit-Reset headers describing the limit that was hit. When every attempted provider returned a retry hint, the error response also carries a Retry-After header. To monitor your remaining free-model daily quota before hitting a limit, call GET /api/v1/key as shown above. It doesn’t report the key-management limit. To resolve errors: Retry with exponential backoff. Rate limits are transient; wait and retry rather than immediately re-sending. Honor the Retry-After header when present. On free variants , purchase at least credits to raise your daily limit, or switch to the paid variant of the model, which has no platform-level request cap. For provider-side limits , add fallback models or relax provider routing preferences so more providers are eligible to serve the request. ​ Mid-stream rate limits If a rate limit is hit after streaming has started, the error arrives as an SSE event with finish_reason: "error" instead of an HTTP , since the status was already sent: data: {"id":"cmpl-abc123","object":"chat.completion.chunk","created":1234567890,"model":"openai/gpt-4o","provider":"openai","error":{"code":429,"message":"Rate limit exceeded"},"choices":[{"index":0,"delta":{"content":""},"finish_reason":"error"}]} See Handling Errors During Streaming for details and code examples. team Frequently Asked Questions Billing and Pricing How are tokens billed? Input and output tokens are billed per model at posted rates. Do you mark up provider pricing? No. Inference is billed at the provider's list price on every plan. OpenRouter's fee is charged when you buy credits, 5.5% on Standard and 8% on Business, never on individual requests. How is billing structured for Standard, Business, Enterprise and BYOK? Standard and Business: you buy credits, manually or with auto top-up, and each request deducts its cost from your balance. The only billing difference between the two is the fee on credit purchases, 5.5% on Standard and 8% on Business. Enterprise: pricing is set by contract and based on volume, prepaid credits and annual commitments, with invoicing. BYOK: the provider bills you for inference directly. Standard and Business include $25,000 of list-price inference per month through BYOK with no OpenRouter fee; Enterprise allowances are custom. Above the allowance, OpenRouter charges 5% of what the same request would cost at list price on OpenRouter, deducted from your credits. Are failed or fallback attempts billed? No. An attempt that errors is not charged for its model tokens, so with fallback you pay only for the run that answers. Under Zero Completion Insurance the same holds for a response that returns nothing and no finish reason; auxiliary services that already ran, such as web search or file parsing, may still be billed. Routing through openrouter/auto adds no fee; you pay the rate of whichever model serves the request. Do you offer volume discounts or annual plans? We offer discounted OpenRouter fees in our enterprise plan. We do not discount inference. Are streaming responses billed differently? No. Pricing is per token whether or not you stream. What payment methods do you accept? Standard and Business: credit and debit cards, AliPay, and crypto (USDC). Enterprise: invoicing and purchase orders through sales. Are taxes (VAT/GST) included in prices? Prices are exclusive of applicable taxes. Where required, VAT/GST may be added on invoices. Is there a minimum spend or lock-in on Standard? No. Standard and Business have no minimums and no lock-in. You pay only for what you use. What does the Business plan fee apply to? The 8% Business platform fee applies to credit purchases. It is charged when you buy credits, not on individual API requests, and model token prices are the same as on every other plan. Do I need to talk to sales to upgrade to Business? No. Upgrade from the settings of the account or organization you want on Business. There is no contract, no minimum spend, and no sales conversation. You can downgrade 30 days after the upgrade, from the same place. Usage and Rate Limits Do you enforce rate limits? OpenRouter sets no plan-based rate limit on paid models. A limit you hit there normally comes from the provider, and fallback routing retries other providers automatically; only very high burst traffic is rejected by OpenRouter's own DDoS protection with a 429. Free models are capped at 20 requests per minute and 50 per day, rising to 1,000 per day once your account has bought at least $10 of credits. Failed attempts count toward that daily cap, and a negative balance blocks free models until you add credits. Details are in the rate limits documentation . Can I separate environments (dev/staging/production)? Yes. Workspaces give each environment its own keys, limits and activity: 5 workspaces on Free and Standard, 1,000 on Business. Within a workspace, each API key can carry its own credit cap. Do you enforce platform rate limits? No plan-based ones. On Standard, Business and Enterprise, limits on paid models come from the provider, not from your plan; only OpenRouter's DDoS protection can reject very high burst traffic. Free models carry the caps in the answer above. Routing and Latency Can I make sure to send API requests in specific regions? Yes. In-region routing is included on Business and Enterprise plans. Send requests to eu.openrouter.ai to keep inference with providers in the EU, or to us.openrouter.ai to keep it in the US. Upgrade to Business from your settings; for Enterprise, contact sales. Does routing affect latency? Routing improves reliability; latency varies by model, provider and region. For consistent latency, pin a specific model and provider. What happens if a model is deprecated or pricing changes? If a model is deprecated, you will receive a 404 when you request it, with an error message like "no endpoints for this model found." If the pricing changes, we will continue to route to the model and it will serve your requests. But, you will be charged at the new rate and your credits will deduct accordingly. This will be reflected in your billing. Can I pin specific model versions? Yes. Choose an explicit model ID/version to avoid unexpected changes. She’s focused on making Lindy the most powerful yet easy-to-use AI workflow automation app. Reviewed by Michelle Liu Last Updated: November 6, 2026 Expert Verified Table of contents H2 Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, and the same day it took the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, but almost nobody can use it yet. Carbon is Google's strongest model, built for long engineering jobs and cybersecurity, and it went to a small group of cyber defenders first while developers, businesses, and Gemini app users wait for a date. I went through Google's launch post and its full benchmark table, Google's November 2 update, Artificial Analysis's results, the Fairwind Program page, the Gemini API docs, the Gemini app release notes, and Google's AI plans page on November 3. Here's what Gemini 4 Carbon is, who can use it right now, what it will cost, how its benchmarks hold up, and what changed from Gemini 4 Argon. TL;DR: What it is: Google DeepMind's newest frontier model, announced October 28, 2026, and built for long-running coding, agentic work, and cyber defense. How good it is: #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 at 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (58) and two ahead of GPT-6 Astra (57). Who can use it: as of November 3, only U.S. government pre-release testers and a subset of cyber defenders in Google's Fairwind Program. More trusted partners come next, then developers, businesses, and consumers "as soon as possible," with no date. Where it isn't yet: the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, the Gemini app, Google Cloud, and every Google AI plan. Price: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens at launch, rising to $4 and $20 after an introductory period Google hasn't dated. Cached input is 95% off. What changed from Argon: 9 points higher on Artificial Analysis, much stronger cyber scores, roughly half the unsupported claims, and 0.0% success for prompt-injection attacks in Gray Swan's test. What is Gemini 4 Carbon? Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's newest and strongest AI model, announced on October 28, 2026, by Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google's Chief AI Architect. Google's launch post describes it as its "strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities." It arrived 15 days after Gemini 4 Argon became generally available, which makes it the second Gemini 4 model in a month. Google says Carbon "illustrates the pace at which we're pushing the frontier forward." Carbon is built for jobs that take a long time. Google says its teams have seen it "run for days," working through dead ends to root-cause and patch subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. The specs, from Google's launch post and Artificial Analysis : 🔧 Spec 📋 Gemini 4 Carbon Made by Google DeepMind Announced October 28, 2026 Who can use it U.S. government testers and a subset of cyber defenders in the Fairwind Program (as of November 3, 2026) API model ID Not published yet Launch price $2 input, $10 output per 1M tokens Standard price $4 input, $20 output per 1M tokens, after the introductory period Cached input 95% off the input price Context window 1 million tokens (per Artificial Analysis) Inputs and output Text, images, video, and speech in, text out (per Artificial Analysis) Open weights No Google hasn't published Carbon's model ID, output limit, or knowledge cutoff, so this table takes the context window and input types from Artificial Analysis. Who can use Gemini 4 Carbon right now? As of November 3, 2026, Gemini 4 Carbon is only available to U.S. government pre-release testers and a subset of cyber defenders in Google's Fairwind Program. It isn't in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, the Gemini app, or Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), and none of Google's AI plans list it yet. Google's launch post describes the rollout this way: U.S. government pre-release testing. Google says it's "actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing." A subset of cyber defenders, starting the week of October 28. Google's November 2 update says this group gets Carbon "via the Fairwind Program," which fits where Carbon's biggest gains are. More trusted partners through the Fairwind Program. Google will "gradually phase access" to them. Developers, businesses, and consumers. Google says Carbon will reach its "product surfaces as soon as possible," after it keeps gathering feedback and iterating on guardrails. On November 3, I checked the places Carbon would show up first. The Gemini API's changelog has no Carbon entry (its latest update, on October 30, is about Computer Use), the API pricing page and models list still top out at Argon, the Gemini app's release notes don't mention Carbon, and Google's AI plans page lists Argon for Google AI Pro and Ultra with no mention of Carbon. One company outside Google's cyber program has said it's coming. Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas posted on October 30 that Carbon is "coming soon to all Perplexity Pro and Max users inside Computer, once we have sufficient token capacity," without a date. Google hasn't confirmed that. For comparison, Argon was announced on September 30 and opened to paid users on October 13, two weeks later. Google hasn't said Carbon will follow the same schedule. How the Fairwind Program works The Fairwind Program is Google DeepMind's early-access program for cyber defenders. Its program page says it gives "high-priority defenders (like governments, healthcare providers, and telecommunications services) early access to advanced models," and that it works with more than 650 partners worldwide. Google prioritizes three groups: Governments and national cyber authorities Critical infrastructure operators in healthcare, telecommunications, energy, and finance Core technology platforms whose software millions of people depend on To apply, Google says to contact your Google Cloud account team. Applicants go through background checks, members can only use the models for defensive and research work, and they can't share or resell access. As of November 3, the program page still describes exclusive access to Gemini 4 Argon and doesn't mention Carbon yet. What to use while you wait Gemini 4 Argon is the closest thing you can use today. It's in the Gemini API for paid developers, and in the Gemini app for Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) and Ultra (from $99.99 a month) subscribers. Our Gemini pricing guide covers the plans, and our Argon explainer covers where it runs. If you need a frontier model in production this week, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra are both generally available and score within two points of Carbon on Artificial Analysis. Gemini 4 Carbon pricing Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, the same introductory price Argon launched at, with cached input tokens priced 95% below the input rate. A footnote in Google's post adds that "the price of $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens will apply" once the introductory period ends. 💵 Price per 1M tokens 📥 Input 💾 Cached input 📤 Output Gemini 4 Carbon, introductory $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 Gemini 4 Carbon, standard $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon, through Nov 30 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 Gemini 4 Argon, from Dec 1 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Carbon's prices come from Google's post and Artificial Analysis, and Argon's come from the Gemini API pricing page. Google hasn't said when Carbon's introductory price ends. Artificial Analysis describes it as a 50% launch discount "with no confirmed end date." Argon's discount runs through November 30, so budget Carbon at $4 and $20 if you're planning past the introductory period. What it costs per task Carbon will cost less per job than Claude Opus 5.5, even though both list at $4 and $20 per million tokens at standard pricing. Artificial Analysis puts Carbon at $7.76 per Intelligence Index task at standard pricing, about 23% less than Opus 5.5 ($10.04), because Carbon writes about 123,000 output tokens per task against Opus 5.5's 173,000. GPT-6 Astra is cheaper still at $6.25 per task, and Argon costs $7.68 at the same $4 and $20 price while scoring 9 points lower. ‍ {{templates}} ‍ Gemini 4 Carbon benchmarks: Google's numbers vs. independent tests Gemini 4 Carbon leads most of the benchmarks Google published, and the independent results back up its overall #1 spot while showing a few areas where it trails. Google's own numbers Google's launch post includes a table of 17 benchmarks comparing Carbon with Argon, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1. Carbon has the top score on 15 of them. Here are the headline results: 📊 Benchmark 🧪 What it tests 🏆 Carbon 📉 Next best SEC-bench Pro Finding real vulnerabilities 88.2% GPT-6 Astra, 85.4% ExploitGym Checking whether a flaw is exploitable 54.8% GPT-6 Astra, 42.4% CWE-bench Patching the root cause 71.0% Argon and GPT-6 Astra, 68.0% Terminal-Bench 4.0 (AA) Multi-step terminal work 65.2% Opus 5.5, 59.6% GraphWalks (256K to 1M) Reasoning over very long inputs 96.2% Argon, 84.2% AutomationBench (Zapier) Business workflows across apps 53.9% Argon, 51.3% Agents' Last Exam v1.1 Computer use 77.4% GPT-6 Astra, 73.1% Vals Index v2.2 Vals AI's overall index 70.4% Opus 5.5, 70.2% "Next best" means among the models in Google's table. On Artificial Analysis's own Terminal-Bench 4.0 leaderboard, Kimi K3.1 Pro edges Carbon, 67.2% to 65.2%. Google ran the three cyber benchmarks without guardrails. It also reports that Carbon jumped 89 Elo points to 1768 on WebDev Arena , which put it at #4 for building websites at launch. Some of Google's strongest claims come from internal testing you can't check. Google says Carbon has more than twice Argon's success rate at generating secure code, and that Chrome's team found it more than 10 times better than "another lab's large frontier model" at writing high-quality patches. What Artificial Analysis found On Artificial Analysis , Gemini 4 Carbon scores 59 on the Intelligence Index v5, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 at 58 and GPT-6 Astra at 57. The index blends nine tests, and Carbon has the top score on four of them: HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, and AutomationBench-AA. Its knowledge results stand out. On AA-Omniscience, which penalizes confident wrong answers, Carbon scores 54 against 48 for Opus 5.5, and its hallucination rate is 11%, among the lowest Artificial Analysis has measured (only Argon and Carbon's own medium setting, both at 4%, are lower). Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra both sit at 50%. SemiAnalysis's GDPx benchmark , which grades 206 hard tasks across 11 fields, tells a value story. Carbon scores 10.9%, just behind Opus 5.5 at 12.0% and ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 9.6%, at $16.29 per task against $51.41 for Opus 5.5 and $53.99 for Astra. As 9to5Google noted , GPT-6 Astra moves to #1 if you drop the cybersecurity, biology, and alignment categories. Artificial Analysis ran Carbon with high reasoning, while Opus 5.5 and Astra ran at max, so treat a one-point lead as close to a tie. Where Carbon doesn't lead Carbon trails in a few areas, and both Google's table and Artificial Analysis show where: Coding agents: on Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index, Carbon in Google's Antigravity CLI scores 59, three points behind Claude Code running Opus 5.5 (62). Computer use: Opus 5.5 wins OSWorld-2.1 in Google's own table, 87.2% to Carbon's 81.5%. Real-world software tasks: GPT-6 Astra wins FrontierSWE 2, 65.5% to 61.2%. Office work: on AA-Briefcase, which tests spreadsheets, slides, and documents, Carbon's 1,610 Elo ranks eighth, well behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (1,814) and Claude Opus 5.5 (1,801). Hallucinations vs. Argon: Carbon's hallucination rate rose from Argon's 4% to 11%, even as it answered 10 points more questions correctly. What changed from Gemini 4 Argon Carbon is a step up from Argon on almost every number Google and Artificial Analysis published, two weeks after Argon reached paying users. Here's what changed: Higher overall score: 59 on Artificial Analysis, up 9 points from Argon's 50. Longer jobs: Google says Carbon is built for "sustained agentic workflows" and has run for days on hard engineering tasks. Better cyber work: more than 2x Argon's success rate at generating secure code in Google's internal tests, plus higher scores on all three cyber benchmarks (ExploitGym rose from 42.0% to 54.8%). Fewer unsupported claims in Google's tests: Google says Carbon cuts unsupported claims by about half compared with Argon, and it adds caveats to its work or lists what's still missing when it lacks evidence. Better scope control: Google says overreach is down 26% and under-service is down 29%, so it does more of what you asked and less of what you didn't. Less cheating on tests: successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 fell to 0.0%, with attempts at 0.4%, and high-severity misalignment alerts in Google's live coding environments dropped by almost 80%. Stronger prompt-injection defense: 0.0% attack success on Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection benchmark, down from Argon's 0.7%. Better web output: up 89 Elo points to 1768 on WebDev Arena. Carbon's pricing mirrors Argon's. It launches at the same $2 and $10 introductory rates Argon had and moves to the same $4 and $20 standard price, so the upgrade costs about the same per task. The one trade-off in the numbers is hallucination. Carbon knows more, but when it's wrong it's more often confidently wrong than Argon was. Gemini 4 Carbon vs. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra Carbon leads overall by a point or two, Opus 5.5 still leads coding agents, OSWorld-2.1 computer use, and office work, and both rivals are available to use today. Claude Opus 5.5 has been on the Claude API and paid Claude plans since September 22, and GPT-6 Astra is generally available too. Carbon will cost less per task than Opus 5.5 at list price and more than Astra. For the full head-to-head, including specs, costs on a real workload, and which to pick for each kind of job, see our Gemini 4 Carbon vs. Claude Opus 5.5 comparison. For how Argon stacks up against OpenAI's flagship, see Gemini 4 Argon vs. GPT-6 Astra . ‍ {{cta}} ‍ Should you wait for Gemini 4 Carbon? Wait for Carbon if your work matches its strengths, and use what's available if you need a model this week. Watch for Gemini 4 Carbon if you: Do vulnerability research, patching, or other security work, where it posts the top scores on SEC-bench Pro, ExploitGym, and CWE-bench Need answers you'll quote, since it has the best AA-Omniscience score and a lower hallucination rate than Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra Work with very long documents or codebases, where it scores 96.2% on GraphWalks at 256K to 1M tokens Run long, multi-step agent jobs that need to stay on task for hours Already build on Argon and want an upgrade at the same price Use something else for now if you: Need a frontier model in production today (Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra are both available) Mostly run coding agents, where Claude Code running Opus 5.5 still leads Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index Want a Google model right away, in which case Argon is in the Gemini API and the Gemini app If you'd rather not track which model wins each week, Lindy , an AI teammate that works in Slack, lets you pick your model for each task from most major models, so you can switch when a new one pulls ahead. FAQ When can I use Gemini 4 Carbon? Google hasn't given a date. As of November 3, 2026, Carbon is limited to U.S. government pre-release testing and a subset of cyber defenders in the Fairwind Program, with more trusted partners being added gradually. Google says developers, businesses, and consumers will get it "as soon as possible." Paying developers can reach Gemini 4 Carbon through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio. Enterprises have access through Gemini for Business and specialized agents including CodeMender and AlphaEvolve. Consumer access is limited to Google AI Ultra subscribers via the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search, and Antigravity. The cited Google announcement does not specify whether Carbon will reach lower-priced tiers or free users. The Introductory Price Makes a Real Case Against Claude Fable Through November 30, Carbon's token rates are roughly one-quarter of Claude Fable 5.2's published standard price. Advertisement Advertisement During the introductory period, Carbon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Claude Fable 5.2 is listed at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, with an optional fast mode doubling those rates. A Pricing Cliff Arrives December 1 Carbon's rates double on December 1, landing it exactly where Claude Opus 5.5 already sits. After November 30, Carbon's standard rates rise to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. At that point, Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 carry identical published prices, and the gap with Fable 5.2 narrows from fourfold to twofold. Benchmark Data Shows a Mixed Picture For latency-sensitive workloads, the gap is significant: Carbon averages 26.1 minutes per task while Fable 5.2 completes the same tasks in 16.9 minutes at high effort. Carbon's estimated average cost per Intelligence Index task is $7.76, against $9.08 for Fable at high effort, making Carbon the cheaper option at that configuration despite the modest performance gap. Effort settings shift the comparison further. Artificial Analysis reports Fable at low effort costs $3.10 per task, against $6.59 for Carbon at medium effort, though those configurations are not directly comparable. Token rates alone do not resolve the question. Task Type Determines Which Model Leads Carbon dominates terminal benchmarks, while Fable holds the advantage on repository-level coding tasks. The better model depends on what a given workflow actually requires. Total Workflow Cost Is the Right Metric Thinking tokens, retries, and reviewer time all factor into what Carbon actually costs to run. The cited Google announcement does not mention downloadable weights or a self-hosting license. Teams evaluating Carbon need to account for token consumption across reasoning steps and task failure rates. Latency against their SLAs and the human time spent reviewing or correcting outputs add further cost. Run the Pilot Before November 30 The introductory window is the right time to generate real cost data, not rely on marketing comparisons. A controlled pilot using identical tasks, tools, permissions, and acceptance criteria will produce more useful numbers than published benchmarks alone. For terminal automation and business workflows that supercharge your productivity , Carbon's benchmark results are competitive or stronger; for repository-level coding tasks, Fable's FrontierCode-AA lead is worth weighing carefully. How to stretch the free quota and avoid 429s Free-tier limits cover requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (TPM) and requests per day (RPD). Cross any one and you get a rate limit error. Five habits keep you under them: Read your real limits per model on AI Studio’s rate-limit page. Don’t add keys. Limits apply per project, not per API key. Plan around the reset. RPD quotas reset at midnight Pacific time. Route by difficulty. Short jobs go to Flash-Lite, harder ones to 3.8 Flash. Back off on 429s with exponential delay instead of a tight loop. Here’s a minimal retry wrapper. The request shape follows Google’s REST quickstart in the Gemini 4 Argon developer guide , and the model name lives in a variable so the same script moves to a paid model later: # Free key: gemini-3.8-flash. Paid key: GEMINI_MODEL=gemini-4-argon. # Google hasn't published a Gemini 4 Carbon model ID yet. MODEL="${GEMINI_MODEL:-gemini-3.8-flash}" for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5; do code=$(curl -s -o out.json -w "%{http_code}" -X POST \ "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions" \ -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "{\"model\": \"$MODEL\", \"input\": \"Summarize this changelog in five bullets.\"}") [ "$code" != "429" ] && break sleep $((2 ** attempt)) # 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 seconds done echo "HTTP $code"; cat out.json Moving to gemini-4-argon ? The free Gemini plan, AI Plus, AI Pro and the Gemini API free tier do not include Carbon. Google has given no date for Pro or free access, and Argon itself still skips the free plan. What Is Gemini 4 Carbon? Release Date and What It's Built For Gemini 4 Carbon is a Gemini 4 model that spends more thinking tokens per turn than Argon. Google's model card puts it plainly: Carbon "is based on Gemini 4 Argon." The extra thinking goes into exploring hypotheses, reasoning longer and running verification loops before it answers. It reached the public in two steps. Carbon is for the jobs that strain a model, such as complex multi-step debugging and open-ended scientific research. Expect slower, longer answers in exchange. If you're on the free plan or AI Pro, nothing Google has published says when that changes. So match the model to the job. Use Argon for everyday coding and writing, and save Gemini 4 Carbon for long multi-step tasks, where the extra thinking pays off. Gemini 4 Carbon: Google's New Model Tops the Benchmarks, Here's the Data | MindStudio Skip to main content Product AI Models AI Media Workbench Agent Skills Plugin Workflow Capabilities Pricing Learn University Documentation Blog About Log in Get Started My Workspace Product AI Models AI Media Workbench Agent Skills Plugin Workflow Capabilities Pricing Learn University Documentation Blog About Log in Get Started My Workspace Blog / Gemini 4 Carbon: Google's New Model Tops the Benchmarks, Here's the Data Gemini 4 Carbon Google Carbon model Artificial Analysis index Gemini 4 Carbon: Google's New Model Tops the Benchmarks, Here's the Data Gemini 4 Carbon hits 59 on Artificial Analysis's index, leading cybersecurity and agentic benchmarks over GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. Edited by Luis Chavez-Mattos , Director of Product · October 29, 2026 · RSS What is Gemini 4 Carbon? Gemini 4 Carbon is Google’s newest frontier model, announced as its strongest offering to date with a specific emphasis on cybersecurity and long horizon agentic tasks. On Artificial Analysis’s newly released Intelligence Index V5, Carbon scores 59, edging out Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 58 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra at 57. It was announced only two weeks after Google’s prior release, Gemini 4 Argon, which scored 50, a jump large enough that Google itself called out the pace of its own progress. TL;DR Carbon leads the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59, putting it narrowly ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (58) and GPT-6 Astra (57) on an aggregate benchmark score built from multiple independent evaluations. Cybersecurity is the headline differentiator , with Carbon posting strong leads on SecBench Pro (vulnerability discovery), ExploitGym (54 versus 42 for Astra and 34 for Opus 5.5), and CWEBench (71) for patching. It’s notably token-efficient , using around 123,000 tokens to complete tasks on the benchmark suite, roughly half of what Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 require and about 20% less than Opus 5.5. Pricing undercuts most frontier competitors at an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising to $4/$20 after an unspecified introductory period, with cached input tokens discounted 95%. Rollout is staged rather than immediate : Google is routing early access through cyber defense partners and its “Frontier Safety” trusted-tester program before general availability, a departure from typical same-day model drops. On the quality-versus-cost tradeoff (the Pareto frontier), OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol models still hold the efficiency crown , needing fewer tokens per task than Carbon even though Carbon scores higher on raw intelligence. Google reports specific alignment fixes , including reducing successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0% and cutting unsupported claims roughly in half compared to Argon. Across the benchmark suite Google published alongside the model, Carbon generally sits at or near the top, though the margins vary by category. On SWE-bench (a coding benchmark), Carbon scores 9.6 compared to Argon’s 4.3, putting it roughly in line with Astra and ahead of both Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which tests a model’s ability to write and execute terminal commands for agentic coding, Carbon hits 65 versus 59 for Argon and Astra, and 52 for Fable. Not every benchmark favors Carbon. On OSWorld, which measures a model’s ability to control a computer, Opus 5.5 actually leads at a higher score, with Carbon in second place at 81.5 and Astra close behind at 80.99. In Vending-Bench, a simulation where models run a vending machine business to maximize profit, Carbon’s $16,000 final balance beat Astra’s $15,000 and outpaced both Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 by a wide margin. Carbon also leads on Agents’ Last Exam at 77.4 and ranks first on both Reman Bench and Terminal-Bench Science, two math and science focused evaluations. Why is Carbon’s cybersecurity performance significant? The most distinct claim Google is making is that Carbon sets a new standard for cyber defense capability. On ExploitGym, a benchmark that tests a model’s ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities, Carbon scores 54 against 42 for Astra and 34 for Opus 5.5. Google also reports leads on SecBench Pro for vulnerability discovery and CWEBench (71) for patching known weaknesses. This matters beyond the scoreboard because models with strong offensive security skills carry real dual-use risk: the same capability that finds a vulnerability for a defender can be used by an attacker. That’s reportedly why Google isn’t dropping Carbon into general availability immediately. Instead, it says it’s working through the U.S. government’s voluntary pre-release testing process and giving early access to cyber defense partners first, with the stated intent being to use the model to find and patch vulnerabilities in existing software before wider release. Google has also said it is actively mitigating “shortcut” behavior, where a model tries to game a benchmark rather than solve it honestly. It specifically says it reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0% and cut cheating attempts to 4%, while also improving overall accuracy and roughly halving unsupported or fabricated claims compared to Argon. Is Gemini 4 Carbon actually more efficient than its rivals? Efficiency here means two separate things: how many tokens a model needs to solve a task, and how much each token costs. Carbon does well on both fronts individually. On token usage, it completes benchmark tasks using about 123,000 tokens on average, compared to roughly 285,000 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and similarly high figures for Haiku 5.5. That’s close to half the token count for a comparable task. Against Opus 5.5 specifically, Carbon uses about 20% fewer tokens. Every team builds with AI. Nothing gets lost. The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today On price, Carbon’s introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens is well below the $5 to $20 input range and up to $50 output range common among top-tier models. After the introductory period (Google hasn’t specified how long that lasts), the price rises to $4 input and $20 output, still competitive for a model performing at this level. Cached input tokens get a 95% discount, which matters a lot for agentic workflows that repeatedly reuse context. But when you plot intelligence score against cost per completed task, the picture gets more nuanced. OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol family occupies the most favorable position on that curve, the “top left quadrant” where quality is high and cost is low. That’s largely because those models use even fewer tokens per task (GPT-6.1 Sol Max reportedly uses around 68,000 tokens, about half of Carbon’s figure). So while Carbon is the highest-scoring model overall, it isn’t yet the most cost-efficient one for a given task. Google will likely need to ship smaller, distilled variants of Carbon to compete across the full price-performance spectrum the way OpenAI currently does. Why is Google rolling out Carbon differently than past models? Most frontier labs announce a model and make it available, via API or chat interface, within a day or so. Google’s pattern with Carbon breaks from that: it announced the model and published benchmark results, but access is being phased in gradually. First come cyber defense partners, then additional trusted testers through what Google calls its Frontier Safety program, and only after that general availability for developers, businesses, and consumers. Google frames this as a deliberate safety step tied to Carbon’s unusually strong offensive security capabilities, paired with engagement in a voluntary U.S. government pre-release testing process. It’s a reasonable explanation given the ExploitGym numbers, though it also means anyone wanting to evaluate Carbon hands-on will be waiting longer than usual after the announcement. Frequently Asked Questions What is the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index? It’s an aggregate score published by Artificial Analysis, a third-party firm that compiles benchmark results from many sources into a single comparative index. Version 5 of that index currently ranks Gemini 4 Carbon first at 59, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (58) and GPT-6 Astra (57). When will Gemini 4 Carbon be publicly available? Google has not given a fixed date. The rollout starts with cyber defense partners and trusted testers through a staged access program, with general availability for developers and consumers planned “as soon as possible” afterward, according to Google’s announcement. How much does Gemini 4 Carbon cost to use? The introductory price is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, increasing to $4 and $20 respectively after an unspecified introductory period. Cached input tokens are discounted 95% off the standard input price. Is Gemini 4 Carbon better than Claude Opus 5.5? It depends on the task. Carbon leads on the overall intelligence index, cybersecurity benchmarks, math and science evaluations, and some agentic tasks like Vending-Bench. Opus 5.5 still leads on OSWorld (computer control tasks) and remains, by at least one account, the preferred model for general use until Carbon sees wider hands-on testing.
